title: Locally Nagata universal catenarity ascends along weakly etale maps
statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be commutative Noetherian rings [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], and let $f:A\to B$ be weakly etale [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. Assume that for every prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset A$ the local ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is Nagata [def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring], and that $A$ is universally catenary [def-exc-excellent-ring]. Then $B$ is universally catenary and for every prime ideal $\mathfrak q\subset B$ the local ring $B_{\mathfrak q}$ is Nagata. Here universally catenary means that every finite type algebra over the ring is catenary: between any fixed comparable primes the lengths of finite prime chains are bounded, and all saturated chains have the same length; a saturated chain admits no prime strictly between consecutive terms.

source.document: Silvio Greco, Two theorems on excellent rings, Nagoya Mathematical Journal 60 (1976), 139–149, DOI 10.1017/S0027763000017190
source.place: Theorem 5.3(iii), printed pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 8–9); proof on p. 147 through Proposition 5.4 and Lemma 5.5. Remark 5.2 for AF = weakly etale. Definitions: Stacks Tags 00NI (definition-catenary), 00NL (definition-universally-catenary), 032R (definition-nagata).

proof.text: For $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}B$, put $\mathfrak p=f^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. Base change $A\to B$ to $A_{\mathfrak p}$ and then localize the target at the prime induced by $\mathfrak q$. The stability lemma and the weak etaleness of localization show that the resulting local map $A_{\mathfrak p}\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ is weakly etale. Explicitly $(B\otimes_A A_{\mathfrak p})_{\mathfrak q^{\prime}}\cong B_{\mathfrak q}$ by $b\otimes(a/s)\mapsto f(a)b/f(s)$; every denominator outside $\mathfrak p$ maps outside $\mathfrak q$. These localizations are Noetherian: every ideal is the extension of its contraction and fractions of finitely many generators of that contraction generate it.

source.document: Silvio Greco, Two theorems on excellent rings (1976), online copy
source.place: Theorem 5.3(iii), first sentence of its proof; Stacks Tags 092H, 092J, 092N for the localized map.

proof.text: The hypothesis supplies that $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is Nagata. Apply Nagata ascent to the Noetherian weakly etale map $A_{\mathfrak p}\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ from step 1. Thus $B_{\mathfrak q}$ is Nagata for each $\mathfrak q$, proving the local Nagata assertion without assuming that $A$ itself is Nagata.

source.document: Silvio Greco, Two theorems on excellent rings (1976), online copy
source.place: Theorem 5.3(iii), first sentence of its proof, and Remark 5.7(ii).

proof.text: Fix $n\geq0$ and write $R=A[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$, $S=B[X_1,\ldots,X_n]=R\otimes_A B$. Both are Noetherian by finite-type Noetherianity, and $R\to S$ is weakly etale by base change. Here the tensor identification sends $h(X)\otimes b$ to $f(h)(X)b$; its inverse sends $\sum b_\alpha X^\alpha$ to $\sum X^\alpha\otimes b_\alpha$, so both composites fix coefficients and variables. Every finite type $R$-algebra is finite type over $A$ (adjoin its generators together with the $X_i$), so $R$ is universally catenary. It is also locally Nagata: for a prime $\mathfrak r\subset R$ with contraction $\mathfrak a\subset A$, $R_{\mathfrak r}$ is a localization of $A_{\mathfrak a}[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$. Its coefficient ring is Nagata by hypothesis, the polynomial ring is Nagata by $n$ applications of polynomial Nagata permanence, and the localization is Nagata. The fraction identification sends $a/s$ to the same fraction and fixes each $X_i$.

source.document: Silvio Greco, Two theorems on excellent rings (1976), online copy
source.place: Proposition 5.4 and the polynomial reduction in the proof of Theorem 5.3(iii); Stacks Tags 00FN, 0334, 032U.

proof.text: For any weakly etale map $R\to S$, distinct comparable primes of $S$ have distinct contractions to $R$. Indeed, base change to the residue field $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)=\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p)$ identifies primes over $\mathfrak p$ with primes of $F=S\otimes_R k$ (first quotient by $\mathfrak pS$, then invert $R\setminus\mathfrak p$). The weakly etale field lemma says that every singly generated $k$-subalgebra of $F$ is finite etale, hence finite dimensional: linear dependence of $1,x,x^2,\ldots$ makes each $x$ algebraic over $k$. Each prime quotient of $F$ is therefore an algebraic domain over $k$, hence a field: for a nonzero $x$, an algebraic equation of least degree has nonzero constant coefficient, and solving it expresses $x^{-1}$ as a polynomial in $x$. Thus all primes of $F$ are maximal, so comparable primes in a fibre coincide.

source.document: Silvio Greco, Two theorems on excellent rings (1976), online copy
source.place: Proof of Theorem 5.3(iii), discreteness of fibres; Stacks Tag 092Q and the explicit algebraic-domain argument.

proof.text: We will use the following elementary consequence of universal catenarity. If $H$ is universally catenary and $T\subset H$ is multiplicative, every polynomial ring $(T^{-1}H)[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]$ is $T^{-1}(H[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m])$, by sending each coefficient fraction $a/t$ to the same fraction and fixing the variables; a common denominator for the finitely many coefficients gives the inverse. The cited localization prime correspondence preserves every interval between its endpoint primes: every intervening prime is disjoint from $T$ because it is contained in the upper endpoint. Thus these polynomial localizations are catenary, since $H[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]$ is catenary. Quotient prime intervals are also unchanged, since every prime between two primes containing an ideal $J$ contains $J$; every finite type algebra over $T^{-1}H$ is such a polynomial quotient. Consequently $T^{-1}H$ is universally catenary. The same finite type argument shows that every quotient of a universally catenary ring is universally catenary; Noetherianity of these rings follows by contracting ideals and extending their finite generators, and by lifting quotient ideals.

source.place: Tags 00NJ (lemma-localization-catenary) and 00NI/00NL (definition-catenary/definition-universally-catenary); written out using the cited general prime correspondence and polynomial presentations.

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak Q\subsetneq\mathfrak Q^{\prime}$ be consecutive primes in a saturated chain of $S$, and put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak Q\cap R$, $\mathfrak p^{\prime}=\mathfrak Q^{\prime}\cap R$. Step 4 gives $\mathfrak p\subsetneq\mathfrak p^{\prime}$. Set $C=R_{\mathfrak p^{\prime}}/\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p^{\prime}}\cong(R/\mathfrak p)_{\mathfrak p^{\prime}/\mathfrak p}$ and $D=S_{\mathfrak Q^{\prime}}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak Q^{\prime}}$. By step 3, $R_{\mathfrak p^{\prime}}$ is Nagata; its quotient $C$ is Nagata by finite-over-Nagata permanence. It is a local domain by the displayed quotient-localization isomorphism. It is universally catenary by the quotient and localization arguments of step 5 applied to $R$. Its normalization in its fraction field is finite by the Nagata and Japanese definitions, taking the trivial finite field extension. Base change $R\to S$ along $R\to C$ to get $C\to C\otimes_R S=(S\otimes_R R_{\mathfrak p^{\prime}})/\mathfrak p(S\otimes_R R_{\mathfrak p^{\prime}})$; send $(r/s)\otimes b$ to $f(r)b/f(s)$ and then localize at the prime induced by $\mathfrak Q^{\prime}$. This gives exactly $D$, since all $s\in R\setminus\mathfrak p^{\prime}$ have image outside $\mathfrak Q^{\prime}$ and the final denominators are precisely those outside that prime. Base-change stability and weak etaleness of localization therefore give a local weakly etale map $C\to D$: the maximal ideals are the images of $\mathfrak p^{\prime}$ and $\mathfrak Q^{\prime}$, and their contraction equality is exactly $\mathfrak Q^{\prime}\cap R=\mathfrak p^{\prime}$. The target is Noetherian local: localizing preserves finite generation of ideals as in step 1, and taking a quotient preserves it by lifting an ideal.

source.document: Silvio Greco, Two theorems on excellent rings (1976), online copy
source.place: Proof of Theorem 5.3(iii), applying Lemma 5.5 to consecutive contracted primes; Stacks Tags 00CT, 032T.

proof.text: The prime $P=\mathfrak QS_{\mathfrak Q^{\prime}}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak Q^{\prime}}$ is minimal in $D$. A prime of $D$ contained in $P$ corresponds to a prime $\mathfrak T\subseteq\mathfrak Q$ of $S$ containing $\mathfrak pS$; its contraction is both contained in and contains $\mathfrak p$, hence equals $\mathfrak p$. Step 4 forces $\mathfrak T=\mathfrak Q$. Prime correspondence also identifies $D/P$ with $S_{\mathfrak Q^{\prime}}/\mathfrak QS_{\mathfrak Q^{\prime}}$: it has exactly the two primes coming from $\mathfrak Q$ and $\mathfrak Q^{\prime}$, so its Krull dimension is $1$. Apply the local component dimension lemma to the map $C\to D$ prepared in step 6 and the minimal prime $P$. It gives $\dim C=1$. Primes of $C$ correspond to primes of $R$ between $\mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak p^{\prime}$; an intermediate prime would give a chain of length $2$, contradicting $\dim C=1$. Thus the contracted adjacent primes are consecutive.

source.document: Silvio Greco, Two theorems on excellent rings (1976), online copy
source.place: Lemma 5.5 and its application in the proof of Theorem 5.3(iii), printed p. 147; Stacks Tag 00E3 for localization prime correspondence.

proof.text: For fixed endpoints $\mathfrak Q_0\subseteq\mathfrak Q_1$ in $S$, contraction sends every finite strict chain between them to a strict chain of the same length in $R$ by step 4. Catenarity of $R$ therefore bounds all these lengths. A finite chain can be refined to a saturated chain by inserting primes; the bound makes this process terminate. Steps 6–7 show that every saturated chain contracts to a saturated chain with the same fixed contracted endpoints. All those chains have the same length because $R$ is catenary. Hence $S$ is catenary. Equal endpoints have only the length-zero chain. If $S$ has no primes the assertion is vacuous.

source.document: Silvio Greco, Two theorems on excellent rings (1976), online copy
source.place: Conclusion of the saturated-chain argument in the proof of Theorem 5.3(iii).

proof.text: Every finite type $B$-algebra is a quotient of some $B[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$, which is catenary by steps 3–8. Such a quotient is catenary: primes of $S/J$ correspond by inverse image to primes of $S$ containing $J$; every prime between two such primes also contains $J$, so the corresponding intervals and their saturated chains agree exactly. The same chain bounds and lengths apply. Thus all finite type $B$-algebras are catenary, which is universal catenarity of $B$. Together with step 2 this proves both assertions.
